{{Nihongo|'''Hideki Shirakawa'''|白川 英樹|Shirakawa Hideki|August 20, 1936 – August 24, 2026}} was a Japanese chemist and engineer who was [[Professor Emeritus]] at the [[University of Tsukuba]] and [[Zhejiang University]]. He was best known for his discovery of [[conductive polymers]]. He was co-recipient of the 2000 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] jointly with [[Alan MacDiarmid]] and [[Alan Heeger]].

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Hideki Shirakawa and Yoshiro Mori 20001018.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|Shirakawa with [[Yoshirō Mori]] (at the [[Prime Minister's Official Residence]] on October 18, 2000)]]

Hideki Shirakawa was born in Tokyo, Japan, on August 20, 1936, the second son of a [[Military medicine|military doctor]]. He was the third of five children.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Shirakawa |first1=Hideki |title=Kagaku ni miserarete |last2=白川英樹 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |year=2001 |isbn=4-00-430709-0 |pages=156 |oclc=47173441}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McClain |first=Dylan Loeb |date=4 September 2026 |title=Hideki Shirakawa, Who Helped Turn a Lab Error Into a Nobel, Dies at 90 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/science/hideki-shirakawa-dead.html |access-date=6 September 2026 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> [[2000 Summer Olympics|Olympic]] [[marathon]]er champion [[Naoko Takahashi]] is his second cousin-niece.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2000-10-12 |title=Chubu Honsha-ban |pages=20 |work=Asahi Shimbun}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=Language problem?  Cousin-niece is not a standard English kinship term.|date=September 2026}} He lived in [[Manchukuo]] and [[Taiwan]] during childhood. Around third grade, he moved to [[Takayama, Gifu]], which is the hometown of his mother.

Shirakawa graduated from the [[Tokyo Institute of Technology]] (Tokyo Tech) with a bachelor's degree in chemical engineering in 1961, and his doctorate in 1966. Afterward, he obtained the post of assistant in the Chemical Resources Laboratory at Tokyo Tech.

== Career ==
[[File:Emperor Akihito Yoshiro Mori and Hideki Shirakawa 20001103.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|[[Emperor Akihito]] conferred the [[Order of Culture]] on Shirakawa (at the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] on November 3, 2000)]]

While working as a research associate at the Tokyo Institute of Technology (Tokyo Tech), Shirakawa studied the synthesis of [[polyacetylene]] using [[Ziegler–Natta catalyst]]s. Earlier preparations of the polymer had produced an insoluble black powder that was difficult to study.<ref name="autobio">{{cite web |title=Hideki Shirakawa – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2000/shirakawa/biographical/ |publisher=NobelPrize.org |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref> In the autumn of 1967, a visiting researcher in his group, Hyung Chick Pyun, used roughly a thousand times more catalyst than intended, apparently because a [[milli]]molar quantity was read as [[Molar concentration|molar]]; Shirakawa later said he could not recall whether the error lay in his instructions or in how they were read.<ref name="autobio"/><ref name="pyun">{{cite web |title=New Insight into the "Fortuitous Error" that Led to the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry |url=https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10432325 |publisher=NSF Public Access Repository |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref> The rapid reaction produced ragged fragments of film instead of the usual powder; by systematically varying the conditions, Shirakawa established that the catalyst concentration was the decisive factor in forming the film, which had a silvery, metallic lustre.<ref name="autobio"/><ref name="nobelpop">{{cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000 – Popular information |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2000/popular-information/ |publisher=NobelPrize.org |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref> He developed this into a controlled method for making polyacetylene films, in which the reaction temperature determined the proportion of ''cis'' and ''trans'' isomers.<ref name="nobelpop"/><ref name="ito1974">{{cite journal |last1=Ito |first1=T. |last2=Shirakawa |first2=H. |last3=Ikeda |first3=S. |year=1974 |title=Simultaneous polymerization and formation of polyacetylene film on the surface of concentrated soluble Ziegler-type catalyst solution |journal=Journal of Polymer Science: Polymer Chemistry Edition |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=11–20}}</ref> Despite its metallic appearance, the film was not a good electrical conductor.<ref name="nobeladv">{{cite web |title=Conductive polymers: Scientific background on the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/advanced-chemistryprize2000.pdf |publisher=Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref>

The film caught the attention of [[Alan MacDiarmid]], a chemist at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] who, with the physicist [[Alan Heeger]], had been studying the metallic-looking inorganic polymer [[polythiazyl]], (SN)<sub>x</sub>; the two met by chance during a coffee break at a seminar MacDiarmid gave in Tokyo.<ref name="nobelpop"/> MacDiarmid invited Shirakawa to the University of Pennsylvania, where he spent a year from September 1976.<ref name="autobio"/> On 23 November 1976, while measuring the conductivity of a polyacetylene film with C. K. Chiang, a postdoctoral fellow in Heeger's group, Shirakawa observed that adding [[bromine]] increased it about ten million times.<ref name="autobio"/> The group went on to show that oxidizing polyacetylene with [[halogen]]s such as chlorine, bromine or [[iodine]], a process they called [[Doping (semiconductor)|doping]] by analogy with semiconductors, could raise its [[electrical conductivity]] by a factor of up to about a billion, higher than any polymer known at the time.<ref name="nobeladv"/><ref name="chemcomm1977">{{cite journal |last1=Shirakawa |first1=H. |last2=Louis |first2=E. J. |last3=MacDiarmid |first3=A. G. |last4=Chiang |first4=C. K. |last5=Heeger |first5=A. J. |year=1977 |title=Synthesis of electrically conducting organic polymers: halogen derivatives of polyacetylene, (CH)<sub>x</sub> |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications |issue=16 |pages=578–580 |doi=10.1039/C39770000578}}</ref><ref name="prl1977">{{cite journal |last1=Chiang |first1=C. K. |last2=Fincher |first2=C. R. |last3=Park |first3=Y. W. |last4=Heeger |first4=A. J. |last5=Shirakawa |first5=H. |last6=Louis |first6=E. J. |last7=Gau |first7=S. C. |last8=MacDiarmid |first8=A. G. |year=1977 |title=Electrical conductivity in doped polyacetylene |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=39 |issue=17 |pages=1098–1101 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.1098}}</ref> Heeger, MacDiarmid, and Shirakawa were awarded the 2000 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] "for the discovery and development of [[conductive polymer]]s".<ref name="nob">{{cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2000/summary/ |publisher=NobelPrize.org |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref> The conduction mechanism is described by the [[Su–Schrieffer–Heeger model]], in which charge is carried by [[soliton]]s;<ref name="ssh1979">{{cite journal |last1=Su |first1=W. P. |last2=Schrieffer |first2=J. R. |last3=Heeger |first3=A. J. |year=1979 |title=Solitons in polyacetylene |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=42 |issue=25 |pages=1698–1701 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.1698}}</ref> after returning to Japan, Shirakawa's spectroscopic studies linked the conductivity of iodine-doped polyacetylene to positively charged solitons.<ref name="autobio"/>

In November 1979, Shirakawa moved to the Institute of Materials Science at the [[University of Tsukuba]] as an associate professor, and he was promoted to full professor in October 1982.<ref name="autobio"/> At Tsukuba he developed methods for synthesizing oriented polyacetylene films using [[liquid crystal]]s as the solvent, and later helical polyacetylene using chiral nematic liquid crystals.<ref name="autobio"/> He chaired the Master's School in Sciences and Engineering of the Graduate School from April 1991 to March 1993, and served as Provost of the Third Cluster of Colleges from April 1994 to March 1997.<ref name="autobio"/> He retired from the university at the end of March 2000.<ref name="autobio"/> In November 2000, he was named a [[Person of Cultural Merit]] and received the [[Order of Culture]].<ref name="autobio"/>

== Death ==
On August 24, 2026, Shirakawa died at a hospital in Yokohama, Japan, at the age of 90.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Japanese Nobel Laureate Hideki Shirakawa Dies at 90; Won Chemistry Prize in 2000 for Work on Conductive Polymers (UPDATE 1) |date=2026-09-03 |url=https://japannews.yomiuri.co.jp/society/obituaries/20260903-346938/ |access-date=2026-09-03 |work=[[The Japan News]]}}</ref>

== Research ==
According the University of Tsukuba's web page on Shirakawa,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. SHIRAKAWA Hideki – University of Tsukuba |url=https://www.tsukuba.ac.jp/en/about/history/nobel/shirakawa/ |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=www.tsukuba.ac.jp}}</ref> his research on [[conductive polymers]] can be broken down into four main categories: [[polyacetylene]] thin film synthesis, the causation of metallic conductivity due to [[Doping (semiconductor)|chemical doping]], the creation of conjugated (double or triple bonds in a molecule which are separated by a single bond) liquid crystalline polymers, and acetylene polymerization development that used liquid crystals as solvents.

# '''Polyacetylene Synthesis''': Polyacetylene was expected to have certain properties, with insolubility making the substance difficult to work with. Dr. Shirakawa found that polyacetylene thin films can be synthesized, and with the thin films, the doctor clarified the molecular and solidified structures of polyacetylene.
# '''Creation of Metallic Conductivity''': Dr. Shirakawa found that, when a trace of a halogen such as bromine or iodine is added to thin film polyacetylene, its electric conductivity increases, and it exhibits metallic conductivity. Shirakawa found that partial electron transfer between dopants and p-electrons of polyacetylene can generate metallic conductivity.
# '''Using Liquid Crystals to Develop Acetylene Polymerization''': Dr. Shirakawa developed a method for the production of highly conductive polyacetylene thin films which paralleled the polymerization of acetylene. Furthermore, he succeeded in the synthesis of thin films of helical polyacetylene whose [[chirality]] is controllable.
# '''Creation of Conjugated Liquid Crystalline Polymers''': Dr. Shirakawa created self-oriented, conjugated liquid crystalline polymers by introducing liquid crystalline groups into the side chains of p-conjugated polymers such as polyacetylene. He also macroscopically oriented the polymers with electric or magnetic fields and succeeded in having the molecules electric anisotropy.

The general definition of electrical anisotropy describes the variation of an electrical property depending on the lateral or vertical direction (x,y,z) in which a current flows.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SURAGUS Everything about electrical anisotropy measurement |url=https://www.suragus.com/en/measurement/electrical-anisotropy/#:~:text=The%20general%20definition%20of%20electrical%20anisotropy%20describes%20the,direction%20(x,y,z)%20in%20which%20is%20a%20current%20flows. |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=www.suragus.com}}</ref>

*2000 – Professor Emeritus of the [[University of Tsukuba]]

*2006 – Professor Emeritus of the [[Zhejiang University]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.zju.edu.cn/englishold/2006/1020/c11993a531485/pagem.psp|title=Nobel Laureate Hideki Shirakawa Appointed as an Honorary Professor-Archives-Zhejiang University}}</ref>

=== The Nobel Prize ===
Shirakawa was awarded the 2000 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] together with [[University of Pennsylvania|UPenn]]'s physics professor [[Alan J. Heeger]] and chemistry professor [[Alan MacDiarmid|Alan G. MacDiarmid]], "for the discovery and development of conductive polymers".<ref>[https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2000/ The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000]</ref> He also became the first [[List of Japanese Nobel laureates|Japanese Nobel laureate]] who did not graduate from one of the [[National Seven Universities]] and the second Japanese [[List of Nobel laureates in Chemistry|chemistry Nobel laureate]].

Over the years, Shirakawa has expressed that he did not want the [[Nobel Prizes]] to receive too much special treatment from mass media (especially the [[Media of Japan|Japanese media]]). He hoped that many vital areas in fields outside the Nobel Prize categories will also become more widely known.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/10/16/national/science-health/shirakawa-unhappy-way-japanese-media-reports-nobel-issues/#.WciWsbIjGJA |title=Shirakawa unhappy with way Japanese media reports Nobel issues {{!}} The Japan Times |access-date=2017-09-25 |archive-date=2017-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170925132527/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/10/16/national/science-health/shirakawa-unhappy-way-japanese-media-reports-nobel-issues/#.WciWsbIjGJA |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Relatives ==
One of his relatives, [[Hitomi Yoshizawa]], is a member of the singing group [[Morning Musume]] ''Morning Girls''. He is also related to [[Naoko Takahashi]], the women's marathon gold medalist of the [[2000 Summer Olympics]].

== Public issues ==
On 6 December 2013, the [[House of Councillors (Japan)]] approved the bill of the [[State Secrecy Law]]. Shirakawa and physics Nobel laureate [[Toshihide Maskawa]] issued a statement saying that the law:
<blockquote>
"threatens the pacifist principles and fundamental human rights established by the constitution and should be rejected immediately''...(omitted)...''Even in difficult times, protecting the freedom of the press, of thought and expression and of academic research is indispensable."<ref>[https://www.science.org/content/article/updated-over-scientists-objections-japan-adopts-state-secrets-law Updated: Over Scientists' Objections, Japan Adopts State Secrets Law | Science | AAAS]</ref>
</blockquote>
